title: Inversions and Figured Bass
intro: A chord keeps its name whichever note is lowest, but the bass note changes how it sounds and how it can be used. Figured bass, the Baroque shorthand, names a chord by its intervals above the bass.

items: Root position: the root in the bass (C E G with C lowest). The most stable.
First inversion: the third in the bass (E G C). Lighter; good for smooth bass lines.
Second inversion: the fifth in the bass (G C E). Unstable in tonal music: the fourth above the bass sounds like a dissonance, so it appears in a few set patterns.
Third inversion (seventh chords only): the seventh in the bass (B♭ C E G for C7).

blocks.text: Only the bass note matters for the inversion. C–G–E–C with C on the bottom is still root position however the upper notes are arranged; the arrangement of the upper notes is the voicing.

widget.title: C major in root position and inversions, then G7 in all four positions

blocks.text: In the Baroque, keyboard players read a bass line with numbers under it and improvised the chords. The numbers give intervals above the bass (compound intervals reduced to simple ones). Modern theory uses the same numbers after Roman numerals:

items: Triads: root position 5/3 (usually written nothing); first inversion 6/3 (written 6); second inversion 6/4.
Seventh chords: root position 7; first inversion 6/5; second inversion 4/3; third inversion 4/2 (or 2).
An accidental alone means the third above the bass is altered; a slash or + through a number means it is raised.

blocks.text: So V6/5 in C is G7 with B in the bass; I6 is C major with E in the bass; ii6 is D minor with F in the bass (a very common pre-dominant).
Because a fourth above the bass is treated as a dissonance, 6/4 chords appear only in four patterns, each with the bass as the guide:

items: Cadential 6/4: I6/4 over 5̂ before V on a strong beat. It is really a dominant chord with two suspensions (the 6 and 4 fall to 5 and 3), so many analysts write it V6/4–5/3.
Passing 6/4: on a weak beat, the bass passing between two positions of the same chord (I–V6/4–I6).
Pedal (neighbour) 6/4: the bass holds while upper voices move to neighbours and back (I–IV6/4–I).
Arpeggiated 6/4: the bass arpeggiates a single chord, as in a waltz accompaniment.

blocks.text: Inversions are what make smooth accompaniment possible. Play C–F–G–C in root position in the right hand and the hand jumps; play C (root), F in second inversion (C F A), G in first inversion (B D G) and C (C E G) and it barely moves. Pianists choose inversions to keep the right hand in one place and let the left hand carry the bass line.

widget.title: I–IV–V–I: jumping versus close voice leading

items: Step 1. Right hand plays C–E–G (root position). Now move the C up an octave: E–G–C. That is first inversion. Move E up: G–C–E, second inversion. All three are C major.
Step 2. Play the progression C–F–G–C with the right hand in root position only: the hand jumps.
Step 3. Now play it with close inversions: C–E–G, then C–F–A (F in second inversion), then B–D–G (G in first inversion), then C–E–G. The hand barely moves.
Step 4. Add the left hand playing the roots C, F, G, C an octave or two below. This is how pianists accompany songs.
Step 5. Step through 'Inversions kept close' on the keyboard above and copy each chord.

blocks.title: Identify
blocks.text: Name the chord and figure: bass F♯, then A, D above it (in G major).
solution: Notes F♯ A D: stack in thirds as D F♯ A, D major. D is V in G. F♯, the third, is in the bass: first inversion, V6.

blocks.title: Figures
blocks.text: Give the figure for a seventh chord with its fifth in the bass, and spell V4/3 in F major.
solution: Fifth in the bass is second inversion: 4/3. In F major V7 is C E G B♭; with G in the bass: G B♭ C E.
